| [NOTE-131](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-131.md) v3 | Schwitzgebel — If materialism is true, the US is conscious | A conditional, informal argument. Any materialist criterion liberal enough to credit rabbits (and rabbit-level distributed aliens, the "squidbits") and behaviourally human-like but oddly built aliens (Sirian supersquids, Antarean antheads) with consciousness also credits the United States. On this argument the US meets the usual materialist marks of consciousness: sophisticated information processing (roughly 10^14 person-to-person visual "connections", comparable to the brain's about 10^14 synapses), goal-directed environmental responsiveness, self-representation and historical embedding. The only exits are eliminativism, extreme sparseness or neurochauvinism, each costlier than the conclusion. The paper argues for no universal criterion. It ends undecided between three readings: US consciousness, a challenge to materialists, or grounds to distrust universal metaphysics of mind. | Read |
| [NOTE-173](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-173.md) v3 | Griesemer & Shavit — Scaffolding individuality (3Cs) | The paper sets out an idealized three-stage sequence of interaction types, which it calls a "first and rough sketch" (§1). Stage 1 is coordination in *collections* (pairwise, "aggregative" interactions of co-located individuals). Stage 2 is cooperation in *conexuses* (a connected web of binary interactions whose benefits can still be counted per member). Stage 3 is collaboration in *communities*: heterogeneous multi-way interactions around a shared goal, in which generatively entrenched "core" interactions give organizational closure. Table 1 puts the transition to a new level of individuality between stages 2 and 3 only. The paper asserts, rather than argues, that this describes evolutionary transitions non-circularly and that individuality is a special case of collectivity. | [NOTE-185](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-185.md) | The moral psychology of obligation | Tomasello proposes that the human sense of obligation is "the internalized social/rational pressure from a joint or collective self-regulating agent 'we'… to do what 'we' expect me to" (§3). | [NOTE-388](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-388.md) | Social ontology: Some basic principles | Searle restates the 1995 theory in twenty pages. He revises the book in two places: status indicators matter in their own right, and some Y terms are free-standing, with no X, as with corporations and money without currency. | [NOTE-389](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-389.md) | Ritchie — Social Structures and the Ontology of Social Groups | A structuralist framework for social groups. | [NOTE-390](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-390.md) | Ritchie — What are groups? | Six criteria for any theory of groups (members vary across times and worlds; groups are temporary, contingent and located; coincident groups of one kind can be distinct) rule out groups as non-singular pluralities, fusions, Burge aggregates and Effingham's sets. | [NOTE-391](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-391.md) | Durkheim — Qu'est-ce qu'un fait social ? | Defines the social fact by exteriority to individual consciousness and external constraint, shown by sanction or by resistance, with diffusion plus independent existence as an equivalent test. | [NOTE-392](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-392.md) | North — Institutions | An essay, not a proof. | [NOTE-393](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-393.md) | Epstein — Social Ontology (SEP) | A survey organised by its author's own distinction: what grounds a social fact versus what anchors the category it falls under. | [NOTE-395](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-395.md) | Hindriks & Guala — Institutions, rules, and equilibria | Institutions are correlated equilibria of coordination games with several equilibria, represented by the players as rules. | [NOTE-405](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-405.md) | Rai & Fiske 2011, relationship regulation | A theoretical review. Moral psychology is the regulation of social relationships: an act is right or wrong according to the relational model participants and observers apply, not according to its harm, fairness or purity in the abstract. | [NOTE-434](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-434.md) | The theory of constructed emotion: an active inference account of interoception and categorization | Barrett's theory of constructed emotion, stated through predictive coding. | [NOTE-455](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-455.md) | The Normative Constitution of Agency | Korsgaard asks whether agency is natural (a movement caused by the right mental state) or normatively constituted (a movement backed by an agent whose unity is achieved by following norms). | [NOTE-553](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-553.md) | Huebner — Genuinely collective emotions | Collective emotion is defended by extending a homuncular, computational account of individual emotion to distributed systems. | [NOTE-736](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-736.md) | Strawson — Intention and Convention in Speech Acts | Austin's thesis that illocutions are conventional fails for warnings, entreaties and objections. | [NOTE-867](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-867.md) | Hutchins — How a cockpit remembers its speeds | In an MD-80 approach, the correspondence between airspeeds and wing configurations for the day's landing weight is computed once, 25 to 30 minutes before landing, by selecting a printed speed card with the displayed gross weight, and is stored in the positions of movable bugs on both airspeed indicators; when the plane slows 10 to 15 minutes later, the needle's approach to a bug cues each flap call by a judgment of spatial proximity. Hutchins argues that this memory belongs to the cockpit as a functional system and that speed bugs do not improve any pilot's memory but replace a recall-and-scale-reading task with a perceptual one. The account is a stylized description of mandated procedure, informed by more than 100 observer flights and simulator recordings, with no measured performance, no comparison of crews with and without bugs, and no failure cases; the claim that the arrangement changes what the system can do is established by analysis of the tasks, not by data. | Read |
| [NOTE-1078](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1078.md) | Sewell — A theory of structure | A reformulation of Giddens's duality of structure. Agency is the capacity to transpose schemas and remobilize resources. A conceptual argument, with a conjecture that depth, more than power, makes a structure durable. | Read |

| [NOTE-1230](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1230.md) | Jaksland — Naturalized, fundamental, and feminist metaphysics all at once | A methodological paper, not an assessment of agential realism as quantum mechanics, which it assumes. Barad holds agential realism to be naturalized metaphysics, justified by quantum mechanics and applied once, to the one reality, whose scope then extends to the lifeworld; she rejects reading it as analogy or as a template that other domains instantiate. That extension is threatened by Newtonian mechanics being a good approximation in the macroscopic domain. It survives only if some ontological features (the subject–object and word–world dualisms, representationalism) are all-or-nothing and admit no metaphysical approximation. Jaksland leaves open whether any do, finds individualism "immediately more agreeable" as something that can obtain by approximation, and argues that even without such features the independence of social theorizing from fundamental metaphysics is contingent (on the size of Planck's constant), not principled. | Read |

| [NOTE-1266](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1266.md) | Being one of us. One is adopting the group's perspective, asking "what should we do?". The other is self-transformation, coming to understand oneself as a member. The first can occur without the second (the discursive dilemma) and the second without the first (toddlers' joint action before age three). Self-transformation is not a belief but a Pushmi-Pullyu representation: "you are a member of us; act as such", at once describing and motivating, triggered by cues such as joint attention, and not under direct rational control. | [NOTE-1288](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1288.md) | Team Reasoning and Intentional Cooperation for Mutual Benefit | Theories of social preference can always fit an observed choice by positing a preference for it, and their non-trivial forms cannot represent trust: on Rabin's intention-based preferences, (send, return) in a Trust Game cannot be common knowledge in equilibrium. Sugden's Schema of Cooperative Team Reasoning aims at a mutually beneficial practice, in which each member gains over her maximin payoff, and binds only when there is reciprocal reason to believe the others endorse it. A market exchange in each party's interest can then be intended as cooperation for mutual benefit. | Read |
| [NOTE-1289](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1289.md) | Second-Person Engagement, Self-Alienation, and Group-Identification | A reconstruction and defence of Husserl's empathy-based account of the "we". Truly social acts need an I–Thou relation of reciprocal, communicative address, beyond even reciprocal empathy. In it I am aware of myself as addressed, and by taking over the other's perspective on me ("self-alienation") the self–other difference stays present but is "somewhat downplayed". That is a formal, necessary but not sufficient, condition of seeing oneself as one of us. "A we, a first-person plural, is not an enlarged I." Zahavi likens it to self-categorization theory's self-stereotyping, replies to Heidegger and Schmid that the "we" can be analysed and that self-awareness precedes in-group bias, and concedes that the face-to-face "we" does not cover anonymous ones. | Read |
| [NOTE-1295](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1295.md) | Reconceptualizing Individuals, Categories, and the Social Group: Self-Categorization Theory 2.0 | An insider's critique and reconstruction of self-categorization theory. The proposed SCT2.0: self-categorization is the categorization of intentional agents; groups are holistic entities triggered by cues to collective intentionality; and relations are propositional, in a language of thought. A theoretical paper; its own evidence is under review. | Read |
| [NOTE-1303](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1303.md) | Enemies with benefits: the dual role of rivalry in shaping sports fans' identity | Stadium-intercept survey at eight Bundesliga clubs in December 2014 (N = 571 after 164 fans with no named archrival were dropped); SEM. | [NOTE-1309](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1309.md) | Being one of us: we-identities and self-categorization theory | A we-identity is held as a group member, is at times salient, is endorsed, and varies in affective salience. | [NOTE-1482](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1482.md) | Bencherki — A pre-individual perspective to organizational action | After Simondon, action is pre-individual: it is not an agent's deed but a difference that contributes to the individuation of persons and organizations at once, and authorship is an outcome. | [NOTE-1484](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1484.md) | Bencherki, Brummans & Vézy — Agency without agents | A conceptual paper. It is expressed in a communicative event in which one process takes up another's excess action, and it may start a collective transindividuation. Agents are its effects, not its sources. It is illustrated by rereading one meeting from Cooren's MSF ethnography. The paper gives a vocabulary for redescription, with no criterion that would let an observation count against it. | Read |
| [NOTE-1489](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1489.md) | Tsoukas & Chia — On organizational becoming | A conceptual paper. It reverses the priority of organization and change. Change is the reweaving of actors' webs of beliefs and habits as they accommodate new experience. It is driven by the radial structure of categories, whose nonprototypical applications extend them, and by human reflexivity. Organization is both the attempt to stem that change and the pattern that emerges from it. Its illustrations are other researchers' ethnographies. Its becoming is carried by human agents. | Read |
